newsitem.title: FRANCE: French car sales rocket in first half of September.
newsitem.headline: French car sales rocket in first half of September.

text.p: New car sales in France surged around 90 percent in the first half of September over year-earlier levels, propelled by the impending expiry of a state rebate scheme, an industry official said on Thursday.

Prior-year sales were weak because a previous incentive scheme expired at the end of June, 1995, and incentives were not reintroduced by the government until last October to underpin the French car market by bolstering weak consumer spending.

Car sales in France totalled 116,585 in September 1995, compared with an average for the month over recent years of 150,000 to 170,000, the chairman of the CNPA, the national council of automotive professions, Jean-Pierre Henaut told reporters.
Car sales have picked up as the September 30 deadline for the rebates approaches. Sales of new cars in France jumped 29.4 percent last month to 172,400.
An industry source said sales this month were expected to rise to around 200,000, a year-over-year increase of more than 70 percent.
Henaut said he expected 1996 car sales in France to exceed two million units, making it the best year for the industry since 1992.
But he said the market could plunge to between 1.5 million and 1.6 million units in 1997 if the rebate programme was not extended.
Henaut's outlook is among the more pessimistic.
Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer this week said he estimated the core French car market, excluding sales driven by special incentives, at around 1.9 million units.
He is not calling for an extension of the rebate scheme on the grounds that the incentives have skewed sales toward less expensive cars with thinner profit margins.

But the chairman of PSA Peugeot Citroen chairman Jacques Calvet has asking the government to either lower the value added tax on car sales or else introduce rebates proportional to the price of the car purchased.
"Mr. Calvet does not think the market will rebound naturally," a company spokeswoman said.

The French carmakers' association CCFA said the incentive programme, which provides rebates of between 5,000 and 7,000 francs for car buyers turning in old clunkers, is tied to nearly a third of recent car sales.

Industry Minister Franck Borotra has said he favoured the incentives, but Finance Minister Jean Arthuis is reported to be opposed to any extension of the programme. The final decision lies with Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

The rebate incentives were first put in place in 1993 by the previous government of Prime Minister Edouard Balladur to jump-start a recovery in the French car industry, which plunged into recession following its best year ever in 1992.
Juppe's government revived the scheme with a few changes last October with the stated aim of clearing the streets of the oldest and dirtiest cars.
